title: Jack Hopkins & Andrey Kovalev: Beyond Toil—Scalable AI-Powered Change Management

segments.text: My name is Andrea Kovalev and together
with my colleague Jack Hopkins, we
represent cloud CISO security
engineering team at Google.
Today we want to talk about a challenge
that every
high velocity engineering organization
eventually turns into. How can we scale
security guard rails without becoming a
bottleneck to product velocity?
Specifically, we're going to walk you
through the use case of how we addressed
the configuration toil review problem
within internal GCP infrastructure
applying our internal AI powered change
management platform.
Here is how talk is structured. I will
start with a scale of the GCP
environment problem statement and talk
about challenges we face every day and
why traditional review models are
hitting breaking point.
Then we will continue with the
description of architecture of our
solution. We will dive under the hood of
the Agentic framework we built and talk
about our dynamic routing, our playbooks
and some engineering solutions we
introduced within our system.
And at the end we will also talk about
evaluation metrics and results which we
achieved running this system in
production and saving hundreds of time
for real human reviewers.
Let's dive into problems space statement
and the scale. So at Google we run more
than 750
different services and applications
within Google cloud platform. Some of
them are internal ones, some of them
like real products which external users
can touch and use. Our team is
responsible for
security of this infrastructure.
We don't want these products to get
hacked and we need to make sure that
every GCP organization,
every project, every folder is secured
and they don't have any path to attacker
to actually take it over.
And if you think about this challenge
and if you compare the numbers then you
can see that
like we have a very huge infrastructure
footprint and we use also infrastructure
as a code as a general model for change
management. So basically when the cloud
product needs to
provision a new piece of infrastructure
or then they need to update their IM
policy or when they need to change their
VPC C perimeter that will create a new
change list or commit into our mono
repository and that change needs to be
somehow reviewed and protected
and Overall
that footprint becomes more than 100,000
changes a year which we need manually
review in traditional space and make
sure that we don't introduce any new
security vulnerabilities or any holes
for attackers which they can use.
What's the problem of doing this
manually? Well, all these services have
different teams and we have a lot of
different standards and practices how
teams can operate. So when a human
reviewer looks at the change, they need
to take into account what standards and
what operational requirements
this particular team has and how they
can actually assess the change properly
and they also need to make sure that
there is no new degradation in terms of
security standards. So we need to make
sure that VPCSC configuration is still
protected and we don't introduce any
weaknesses. We need to make sure that
any identities don't get over permissive
roles and don't get like new credentials
which they not supposed to get and we
need to make sure that overall the
infrastructure is secure.
That requires at least 15 minutes for a
human reviewer to take a look into the
ch change and make a conclusion if there
is anything potentially dangerous there
or not. And manually that's just not
scalable.
So we decided to build a new platform
which is integrated within our internal
infrastructure and internal systems
which allows us to review all of these
changes using AI powered capabilities.
So we build an agentic workflow which
basically integrated with our ticketing
system and our change management system
that can review all the changes, collect
appropriate context. Uh analyze code,
analyze design documents if they are
presented or even search for them and
figure out if this change is somehow
dangerous. introduce any new
vulnerabilities or just deviates from
compliance requirements or standards
which we have in our team.
Overall this system reduces the toil for
reviewers but we still keep human in the
loop. So at the end of the day this
system collects a lot of context and
provides recommendations. The final
decision basically still uh the final
decision still is made by people. Uh but
what we figure out applying this
technology that it helps us to save a
lot of time and basically reduce the
manual toil overall.
the way how it works under the hood. Uh
it's basically like the system of
different agentic workflows and I will
hand over to Jack to describe them.
Thank you Andre. So our platform is
really defined by four key components.
The first of which is the triage agent.
This is the entry point for all incoming
changes. So this could be code reviews,
this could be tickets, this could be
documents, any type of change. this is
going to be the entry point. And so what
the triage agent's job is is to take
this incoming request and generate a
summary from that. So if we have an
incoming ticket, we need to find out who
filed this ticket, who did they file it
to, what information is in the ticket.
And the reason that we need that is
because the next place that the request
goes is over to the router. So what the
router's main job is is to figure out
which workflow to send this to. So, we
have multiple different teams that have
multiple different configurations and
stored and they're stored in these
workflow text proto files. So, what
these are is essentially a step-by-step
guide for how to review one of these
changes. And so, since we have multiple
teams with multiple workflows, we need a
trigger. And so, what the router does is
it loads every workflow. It looks at the
triggers for each and every workflow and
it's going to figure out where to send
this request. So if we have an incoming
ticket and we see that it's assigned to
a certain team, we might define our
trigger as any tickets that are assigned
to this team go through this workflow.
Once we figured out which team it goes
to, we start the evaluation process. So
the evaluation process is a playbook
driven policy reasoning engine as we
call it. Basically what this is is we're
going to read playbooks to determine how
to evaluate these changes. So each step
in the playbook or each step in the
configuration, we can define certain
things. We can define tools that that
stage is allowed to use. We can define
playbooks that it's allowed to call. And
we can define inputs and outputs that
are needed. So what this allows for is
anybody can write these policy
configuration files that define how to
execute this workflow, define a
playbook, and they can use an agent to
simplify this process. Once it's done
with the evaluation, we'll move on to
the action modules. So this is
deterministic code which is designed to
take state changing actions. We don't
just tell the agent, hey, go ahead and
comment on this ticket. Go and approve
this. We don't allow the agent to just
do whatever it wants. And so what we've
done is we've built these deterministic
modules that when the evaluator says,
hey, I've gone through my playbook and
it looks like I need to leave a comment
on this ticket, we tell the action
module, here's the comment I would like
to post. And the action module takes
care of actually making that state
changing um action. So the next thing
I'll talk about is our conditional
execution. So to take a step back here,
when we initially built this pipeline to
deal with a certain set of changes, it
was a very rigid pipeline. It was look
and see if there are any changes. If
there are, make a decision and then
output that decision. It was very simple
and rigid. And so the first thing that
we came across is we realized that we
don't always need to do all three steps.
If there are no new tickets, we don't
need to do any evaluation and we
certainly don't need to output anything.
So what we did is we would stop the
execution if we found that there are no
new tickets. But as we started to expand
these workflows into more advanced
things with more and more steps, we
found that these conditional execution
statements can work for a variety of
different things. So if you have an
advanced, you know, workflow where you
have 10 different steps, you might not
want to evaluate every single step if
certain preconditions aren't met. And so
we do this by passing JSON objects back
and forth between the steps. And so we
ran into a problem. The problem was that
when you tell an LLM to generate JSON,
it doesn't always do exactly what you
want. Um, sometimes you'll say, "Hey,
give me this JSON objects." And it will
say, "Okay, here's the JSON object." We
don't want that. We don't need this
conversational filler. We don't need
anything like that. And so what we did
was we built this hook that runs in
between each step that's going to
extract the longest JSON string so that
we can pass back and forth the decisions
between the agents cleanly.
So the next piece that I'll talk about
is our internal playbook tool. So this
is very very simple. All this is is that
it's a tool that allows us to read
internal playbooks. But this is really
the brain of the whole operation. This
is the glue that brings everything
together across Google. There are a lot
of different playbooks for a lot of
different teams doing a lot of different
things. We don't have to reinvent the
wheel. We already have humans that are
doing these processes and they've
defined these in these markdown files.
So what we do is we simply give our
agent access to read these different
playbooks. So, and what we've also done
is we've scoped what playbooks the agent
is allowed to read. It's very easy for
the agent to start going down rabbit
holes or burn a bunch of contexts
looking through bunch of different
documentation, documentation that might
be out of date. And so, we're very
strict with what the agent is allowed to
call. So, we'll do kind of an end toend
walkthrough of what the architecture
looks like. So, right now there are
basically two input sources. You can
call it via an API or a scheduled chron
execution. So let's say we're going down
the path of a scheduled crown execution.
At the top of the hour, the agent kicks
off. And so let's say Jack has filed a
ticket and he says, "Hey, I would like
to give a disallowed permission to a GCP
service account." So the service or the
triage agent is looking at all incoming
changes and it says, "Hey, I've been
assigned this ticket." So what I need to
do now is I need to generate a summary
of what this incoming request is. And so
it says, "Hey, it looks like Jack has
filed this ticket. It looks like he's
filed it with the cloud security team
and it looks like he's trying to make an
AM change. So, it's going to send that
to the router. Again, the router is
going to look at its list of triggers.
Do we have a trigger that's triggering
on IM changes or tickets for the cloud
security team? If we find it, then we'll
pass it to the next stage, which is the
evaluator. So, now we have in this
example, we'll say a three-step
workflow. The first thing that we want
to do is we want to read over the ticket
and see what my use case is. This is a
disallowed permission. Why am I trying
to use it? Do I have a valid use case
for using it? And so based on the
playbook that we load in, we're going to
be able to instruct the agent how to do
this. As it stands, we currently have
humans that operate this process. We
have extensive detailed information on
how a human should make the
determination if this is actually a
valid use case. We just give the agent
that same playbook and the agent uses
that same evaluation. So in this
evaluation phase, the agent typically
has read only tools. So in this case, it
would be able to read the playbooks. It
passes it on to the next stage, stage
two, which is when we want to st take a
state changing action. But there's a
condition. We want to have an input
condition that wants to make sure that
we have a valid use case. If that's
true, then we'll move on to the next
stage, which might be responding on the
ticket with a with a comment that says,
"Hey, we've reviewed your we've reviewed
your request and this is approved." But
we don't do this via the evaluation um
the evaluator. We send this off to the
action router where it has controlled
execution. Again, we have deterministic
code that says the evaluator said, "Hey,
based on my playbook, here's the comment
I need to post." We send it to the
action router and the action router is
what takes that comment and posts it.
So, we're not allowing the agent to do
whatever it wants. Then, the last stage
might be if if we're, you know, defining
these AM policies via uh infrastructure
as code, we'll actually approve the the
code request. So, this will again will
be sent over to the action router and
then we will have a deterministic piece
of code which will actually do that
review. And so we have this agent with
its own identity which can grant
approvals on certain things which we've
deemed to be allowed.
So
let's look at the metrics. Does this
actually work and how are we defining
success? So the first thing that we're
defining as success is out of scope
detection. Our team ended up with a lot
of toil because we would get a lot of
requests that were out of scope. It was
very difficult to determine what
requests should go to what team. And so
the first thing that we wanted to do was
eliminate all of this out of scope or
all of this out of scope request that
our team was handling. It was burning a
bunch of engineering time for no reason.
So this was the first big win for us.
And if we could drive this number down,
that would be great. And so we were able
to drive it down essentially to zero by
using a playbook to aggressively define
what our actual scope is. The next is
the mean response time. So due to
different factors with close time, it
can be complicated. There are different
time zones we have to go back and forth,
but mean response time is something that
we can easily control. Once we get a
ticket, can we respond within 20
minutes? And so this is what our goal
was to respond within 20 minutes and
we've been able to achieve this. And
then last is the accuracy. None of this
matters if the agent doesn't actually do
a good job. So how are we actually
defining if the agent is doing a good
job? And the way that we're doing it is
by humans going in and reviewing to make
sure that the agent did what a human
would do if they were in the same spot.
So here are some metrics that we've
gathered based on our own team's
execution of this agent over about the
past 12 months. This is only our team
using it for only one process. And so
it's been about 90% accurate. So about
90% of the time, whatever the agent
decided, we had a human go in and review
after the fact. And the human confirmed
that the agent made the right decision
about 90% of the time. And that other
10% of the time, if the agent does not
make the right decision, we will go in
and update the playbooks that the agent
is using to ensure that the next time
around the agent will make the right
decision. And so over time, this
accuracy number will tick up further as
we improve the accuracy of the
playbooks. The next is hours saved. So
in our case, it's not a great number of
hours saved because again, we're only
using this for one workflow in our case
that we're presenting today. But our
engineering team um this was a small
piece of our workflow and so we were
able to automate a about 200 hours over
in our first year or so. Um and then the
last thing is escalations. So about 33%
of the time the agent has escalated to
humans which we actually consider to be
a very good thing. These are times when
the agent looks at the playbook, it
looks at the request and it deems, hey,
I'm not sure that my um I'm not sure
that my playbook tells me exactly how to
evaluate this or this or this request
deems or this request carries enough
risk that this needs to be reviewed by a
human.
So using the power the reasoning ability
of LLM, deterministic Python code, and
uh playbooks that are already written by
humans, we're able to solve a a great
deal of toil for our team. And we hope
that this can help you too. and we're
happy to take any questions.

questions?

>> Yeah, as you mentioned about 90%

do you plan to address as that
percentage gets closer and closer to
100% the tendency of humans to just go
with it? Yeah, so that's a really good
question. So at this time we still have
a human in the loop for most for most,

And so we definitely do deal with humans
kind of trusting the agent more and more
as we get into that. Um especially as we

we have the agent gather information

information from the playbook what the

faced several challenges during the

system and we improved the system

uh another thing I would say was
